questions.prompt: A team says its signup page is neutral because it uses plain text and no recommendation. Which response fits choice architecture?
choices: The page still has architecture because order, grouping, and defaults shape what users notice.
The page becomes neutral if every option uses the same font, color, and button size.
The page avoids architecture only when the team removes examples and helper text.
questions.explanation: Choice architecture exists whenever options are presented. The near-misses treat neutrality as a style choice, but order and grouping still steer.

questions.prompt: A retirement form comes with one savings rate already selected. Which reading best follows from the default effect?
choices: The selected rate is only a placeholder because workers can change it before submitting.
The selected rate is fair if the form gives all options the same amount of text.
The selected rate needs care because many workers may accept what is already chosen.
questions.explanation: Defaults matter because people often stay with the preselected outcome. The other choices miss how inaction can shape real consequences.

questions.prompt: A pharmacy team tests a refill form and sees patients enter a weekly dose in a daily field. Which fix best shows expect error?
choices: Add longer instructions above the field so careful patients can avoid the mistake.
Ask patients to confirm they read the label before the form accepts the entry.
Catch the odd entry before submission because the mistake is predictable.
questions.explanation: Expect error means designing for predictable slips. Longer instructions and attestations still blame the user when the interface could catch the problem.

questions.prompt: Hayes sends money through a transfer app, but the screen gives no success or failure message. Which change best uses feedback?
choices: Keep the screen quiet so users learn to check their account history.
Show a clear confirmation or failure notice while the action is still fresh.
Add a help article that explains where completed transfers usually appear.
questions.explanation: Feedback tells people whether they succeeded or failed. The other answers hide the signal or move it away from the moment of learning.

questions.prompt: A health plan page lists premiums, deductibles, and copays, yet workers still cannot tell which plan fits. What is missing?
choices: More plan facts in the same table so workers can study the full market.
A shorter table that removes technical terms and hides unusual costs.
A map from each plan label to the costs workers will actually face.
questions.explanation: Mappings connect options to lived consequences. More information alone can still fail if it does not answer the chooser's real tradeoff.

questions.prompt: Mia wants the benefit of the smaller jam table without dropping products from the store. Which layout fits the evidence best?
choices: Keep all jams available, but present a smaller front set with clear flavor groups.
Remove most jams from the store so shoppers cannot get stuck comparing them.
Display every jam at once because the full assortment gives shoppers the clearest freedom.
questions.explanation: Structuring complex choices can preserve options while easing search. The near-misses confuse structure with either removal or overload.

questions.prompt: A restroom manager can add another warning sign or print a small target where aim matters. Which result should the manager expect?
choices: The small target can work because it redirects attention at the moment of action.
The warning sign should work better because it explains the desired behavior.
Neither change should matter unless it adds a penalty for poor behavior.
questions.explanation: The Schiphol fly shows that a salient cue can change behavior without persuasion or punishment. The other answers overrate lectures and penalties.

questions.prompt: Harold reviews a checkout page that mentions a late fee only after the order is submitted. How should he read that cost?
choices: The fee can guide behavior because users know costs may appear in checkout flows.
The fee is weak as a guide because the chooser cannot see it at the choice point.
The fee should stay hidden so users focus on the product instead of the penalty.
questions.explanation: Incentive salience means costs and benefits must be visible to shape choice. Hidden or delayed costs often fail as guides.

questions.prompt: A designer wants to avoid paternalism by refusing to arrange the options at all. Which answer best fits the hard edge?
choices: Refusal works if users can sort the options after the page loads.
Refusal still designs something because options must appear in some order.
Refusal is safest when every option is shown without defaults or grouping.
questions.explanation: Design is inevitable because options cannot be presented without some order, grouping, or default. Avoiding the issue does not avoid responsibility.

reviewCards.front: How would you restate bounded rationality (Ch 1) in your own words, then use it on a choice architecture problem?
reviewCards.back: Bounded rationality means people use limited attention and shortcuts, so they make patterned mistakes. Choice architecture uses that fact by arranging defaults, cues, and feedback around the errors people are likely to make.

reviewCards.front: What is choice architecture in plain words?
reviewCards.back: Choice architecture is the setup around a choice: the menu, order, default, warning, cue, and form. It matters because those features shape what people notice before they act.

reviewCards.front: Why does a default need justification?
reviewCards.back: A default decides what happens when someone does nothing. Since many people stay with preselected options, the default should fit likely welfare and make switching easy.

reviewCards.front: How does expect error differ from blaming the user?
reviewCards.back: Expect error assumes some slips are predictable, so the system should catch them. Blame waits for the mistake, then treats confusion as the user's fault.

reviewCards.front: What do mappings add that raw information does not?
reviewCards.back: Mappings connect labels to lived results. They show what an option means for money, time, risk, or care instead of leaving the chooser to decode technical terms alone.

reviewCards.front: How can a smaller front menu preserve freedom?
reviewCards.back: It can keep all options available while grouping or filtering what appears first. The chooser gets less comparison work without losing the ability to search deeper.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice a Setup Check: look at one choice and ask what the setup is doing before anyone decides. Name the default, the likely error, the feedback, the mapping, the menu structure, and the visible incentive.

ifThenPlans.context: A form has a box already checked or an option already selected.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a default is doing work, then run a Setup Check and state what inaction will choose.

ifThenPlans.context: A mistake would be easy to make and costly to repair.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the same slip would catch a tired person, then run a Setup Check and add a catch before submission.

ifThenPlans.context: A label is accurate but still hard to use.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a label makes the chooser translate alone, then run a Setup Check and map it to a lived cost.

ifThenPlans.context: A menu is large enough that comparison becomes the work.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the menu is wearing people out, then run a Setup Check and group the options before showing all of them.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, the first time you touch your wallet, use a Setup Check on one choice you often miss. Count 3 cues, name the error, and change one default, label, or order.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For this week, change one thing in your space that shapes a recurring choice. Put the better option first, make the cost visible, or group a messy set. Watch what changes.

memorableLines.text: Every choice has a frame.
A smaller menu can give back freedom.
Defaults spend attention on your behalf.

chapters.title: Save More Tomorrow
chapters.hook: You open payroll to fix one box, and your future paycheck is already voting.
chapters.counterintuition: The freer plan can be the one with a preset path: a 401(k) form nudges you, even when every option stays yours.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before you send your next reply, rehearse one question with the person nearest the choice: "What would make saying no easy here?" Then listen.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A good savings nudge makes the helpful path easy, pairs future raises with future saving, and keeps refusal simple enough to use.

breakdown.fastRead: You are staring at a payroll page, trying to answer a question that feels too large for a lunch break: why is it so hard to save for a future you still care about? Richard Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi saw the snag inside the 401(k) form. You may want more saving later, but a smaller paycheck today hurts now. Save More Tomorrow moves the yes to a future raise, so the first step does not feel like a cut. A default is a decision with a head start. The lesson is not that workers are foolish. It is that payroll already has a path for delay, and that path can either leak future money or help it grow.
breakdown.deepRead:
Tomorrow is easier to promise than today. That is the engine under Save More Tomorrow: the plan asks for a future commitment, then lets payroll raise the saving rate when pay rises later. The worker still has a choice, but the painful part is moved away from the current paycheck. If you have ever kept a subscription because canceling took too many clicks, you know the shape of the problem. Friction can drain money quietly, even when nobody forced you to keep paying.

Brigitte Madrian and Dennis Shea show the companion move through automatic enrollment in a 401(k). When enrollment requires an extra step, delay picks an answer. When enrollment is preset and exit remains open, the easy path changes. The design levers here are defaults, automatic enrollment, future escalation, and opt-out freedom. Each one handles a different part of the same messy choice. Defaults set the starting line. Automatic enrollment keeps delay from choosing nonparticipation. Future escalation links more saving to later pay. Opt-out freedom keeps the whole thing from becoming a shove.

This is why more paper is not enough. A thicker benefits packet may disclose every rule and still leave Valentin unsure what a small payroll change means for his later life. Better mapping means the form makes the consequence easier to see: choose this path now, save more when pay rises later, and leave if it no longer fits. The nudge works when it helps your own future plan survive today's friction.
breakdown.fullRead:
Natalie reads the opt-out line twice because the sentence is short but the consequence is not. She can stay in automatic enrollment, step into Save More Tomorrow, or leave the 401(k) path alone for now. The form is doing what every form does: it chooses an order, a default, and a level of hassle. The only honest question is whether that design serves the chooser, not whether design can be avoided.

That is the hard edge. Save More Tomorrow is not a license for a planner to chase any average result that looks better on a chart. Automatic retirement escalation is justified only when it improves welfare by the chooser's own lights. If Natalie would want more retirement saving once the current squeeze passes, a future raise is a smart time to ask for the increase. If Griffin can exit with a clear click, a phone call, or a simple form, the nudge has kept its promise. An opt-out matters only when exit is real.

The live danger is hidden pride in good design. A benefits team can fall in love with higher participation and stop asking what refusal feels like. That is where Thaler and Sunstein's liberty claim earns its keep. The worker should not need expert help, social courage, or a lost afternoon to say no. If the default is easy to enter but hard to leave, the plan has changed character. It may still raise saving, but it no longer has the same defense.

The idea also respects why people delay. Retirement is a rare choice. Feedback comes years later. The menu can be full of fund names that mean little at the moment of decision. Earlier nudge conditions fit this case almost too well: hard choice, delayed feedback, weak mapping, and little practice. That does not make workers helpless. It means the setting is asking ordinary people to do a hard thing while they are busy, tired, and looking at take-home pay.

So the practical test is simple: who benefits from the path of least resistance, and can the chooser leave that path without a fight? Ask that before you praise a default. Ask it before you remove one. Save More Tomorrow earns its name only when it lets a person protect future income without feeling poorer today.

Here is the counter-case. If Natalie is short on rent and a late fee is due before payday, obeying the escalation path would be a mistake. The right nudge then is not more saving tomorrow. It is an easy exit today, followed by a clear way back when the squeeze has passed.

examples.title: Valentin's Payroll Memo
examples.scenario: The benefits lead is out, and Valentin, usually the payroll clerk, gets the draft memo. He writes: "Richard Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi call this Save More Tomorrow. The 401(k) increase starts with a future raise, not today's check. Say yes now, and payroll lifts saving later. Say no, and the form must make that plain."
examples.whatToDo: Valentin rewrites the memo around the worker's felt problem. He names the future raise, the later payroll increase, and the plain no before sending it back.
examples.whyItMatters: The memo works because the action lives in payroll, not in a lecture. The worker sees how saving can rise without making today's check smaller.

examples.title: Jules and Griffin Set Defaults
examples.scenario: Jules is keying the default into the benefits screen while the preview still spins. He leaves 401(k) enrollment unchecked, sure that active choice proves freedom. Across the table, Griffin follows Brigitte Madrian and Dennis Shea: automatic enrollment is preselected, and the exit link sits beside it. Jules gets clean consent on paper. Griffin changes what delay selects.
examples.whatToDo: Griffin keeps refusal visible while making enrollment the starting point. Jules records a choice process that treats silence as if it had no effect.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast shows the cost of a blank default. Delay is not neutral when one screen leaves workers out and the other starts them saving.

examples.title: Rosalie's Jammed Portal
examples.scenario: The portal button sticks under Rosalie's thumb, and the help desk line behind her keeps growing. "I cannot sell a smaller paycheck," she says. Imogen turns the monitor back to the 401(k) script and names Thaler and Benartzi's move. "Do not ask today's paycheck to carry tomorrow's wisdom. Ask the next raise to carry it, and keep the no easy."
examples.whatToDo: Rosalie changes the script. She explains future escalation through the next raise, then points to the opt-out step before anyone asks.
examples.whyItMatters: The coach talk keeps the nudge honest. A future yes helps only when the worker also sees a usable no.

examples.title: Skylar's Onboarding Question
examples.scenario: The projector hums so loudly that Skylar misses the first line of the onboarding exercise. The worksheet says a 401(k) box can arrive prechecked. "Isn't that choosing for me?" Skylar asks. The trainer points to Madrian and Shea's finding: automatic enrollment changes what happens when a tired person postpones, and the lesson is the open exit.
examples.whatToDo: Skylar repeats the rule in plain words: the preset path handles delay, but the exit must stay clear enough for a new worker to use.
examples.whyItMatters: The classroom confusion is useful. It separates steering from trapping, which is the line a savings nudge cannot blur.

examples.title: Natalie's Raise Later
examples.scenario: Natalie sets the pen beside the raise letter and leaves the 401(k) form untouched. Months earlier, the same question meant less take-home pay right away, and she slid it into a drawer. This time the text thread from payroll says the increase can begin with the raise. She writes back, "Yes, if the opt-out stays easy."
examples.whatToDo: Natalie accepts the future escalation because the timing changed. She also asks for the refusal step in writing before she treats the yes as settled.
examples.whyItMatters: The before and later view shows the mechanism. The same saver can act differently when the plan removes the visible pay cut.

examples.title: Imogen Tests the Exit
examples.scenario: The opt-out was already buried in the benefits phone script by the time plan designer Imogen heard the complaint. "If Richard Thaler would call this a nudge, why hide the no?" she asks. Valentin answers, "Because enrollment rises when exit is quiet." Imogen says, "Then we are measuring the wrong thing. Put the no where a busy worker can find it."
examples.whatToDo: Imogen makes the team test refusal as carefully as enrollment. Valentin moves the opt-out link beside the automatic 401(k) enrollment line.
examples.whyItMatters: The dialogue protects the hard edge. A nudge can favor saving, but it loses its defense when exit depends on patience or insider knowledge.

questions.prompt: Valentin says the 401(k) menu is fair because every worker can pick any rate. Jules thinks the plan still needs Save More Tomorrow. Who has the better read?
choices: Valentin is right because formal options remove the savings problem.
Jules is right because later commitment can make saving usable.
Valentin is right because payroll should avoid steering workers.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 says the problem remains when people want to save more later than now. The bare menu answer misses the timing and payroll friction.

questions.prompt: Griffin is testing a 401(k) enrollment screen that is preselected but puts a clear exit beside it. What result should he expect?
choices: More workers will stay with enrollment because it is now the easiest path.
Workers will ignore the default because only direct persuasion changes behavior.
The default will matter only after each worker reads every fund description.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 says defaults work by changing the path of least resistance. Direct persuasion and full reading are not the only routes to behavior.

questions.prompt: At onboarding, Skylar leaves the 401(k) form for later, assuming no choice has been made. Which response fits the savings problem?
choices: Delay usually leaves a default or status quo to act in the meantime.
Delay keeps the choice open without changing the worker's path.
Delay improves the choice by giving the worker more time to think.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 treats Skylar's delay as an active savings setting. While she waits, some default remains in force and shapes the outcome.

questions.prompt: Rosalie wants employees to see what a future payroll increase means for later saving. Which revision best follows the mechanism?
choices: She adds a longer disclosure packet so every rule is available.
She links the future raise to the later saving change in plain terms.
She removes the payroll example so workers make a cleaner free choice.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 favors clearer mapping, not more paper by itself. The raise link helps workers compare today's choice with later welfare.

questions.prompt: During a benefits audit, a team likes automatic enrollment but makes refusal require a hard-to-find form. Which criticism lands?
choices: The design should be accepted if average saving rises.
The design should be accepted if the default is disclosed somewhere.
The design needs a realistic exit before the nudge stays defensible.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 says opt-out freedom matters only when refusal is practical. Higher saving or hidden disclosure cannot carry the liberty claim alone.

questions.prompt: Natalie is writing a benefits training note for new payroll staff. She needs one real case to ground automatic retirement escalation. Which anchor belongs in her answer?
choices: She can use any workplace story where a worker delays paperwork.
She can use a made-up saver if the payroll details sound realistic.
She can use Richard Thaler and Save More Tomorrow in a 401(k).
questions.explanation: Fact 6 names Richard Thaler as a real-world anchor with observable design features. A generic or invented story is weaker grounding.

questions.prompt: Imogen says one Save More Tomorrow story is enough to prove the whole point. Griffin pushes back. What is his stronger reason?
choices: Madrian and Shea give an independent 401(k) anchor for the same design problem.
Madrian and Shea replace future escalation with a separate investing lesson.
Madrian and Shea show that all 401(k) menus work the same way.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 says Brigitte Madrian supplies a second anchor, reducing one-story overfit. It does not erase the earlier case or make every menu identical.

questions.prompt: Jules wants the payroll default to maximize the designer's favorite outcome. Rosalie says that misses the standard. Which standard fits?
choices: The designer may choose any outcome if the form is clear.
The designer may favor the outcome that is easiest to measure.
The nudge should track welfare by the chooser's own lights.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 draws the line between chooser welfare and designer preference. Clarity and measurement do not justify improving the designer's favorite result.

questions.prompt: A manager says nudges and mandates are the same once both raise retirement saving. Which reply fits the nudge frame?
choices: They are the same when the worker would probably benefit.
They differ when the preferred path remains avoidable.
They differ only when the worker notices the form.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 says Save More Tomorrow fits the nudge frame because the preferred arrangement remains avoidable. A mandate carries heavier penalties or removes alternatives.

reviewCards.front: Why does Save More Tomorrow ask for a future commitment instead of a bigger cut today?
reviewCards.back: A current pay cut hurts now, even when future saving sounds wise. Save More Tomorrow pairs the increase with a later raise, so saving rises without making today's paycheck feel smaller.

reviewCards.front: How does a default change behavior without arguing with the worker?
reviewCards.back: It changes the easiest route. Under complexity, many people accept the path already set for them, so a preset 401(k) enrollment can matter even without a speech.

reviewCards.front: What makes opt-out freedom real rather than decorative?
reviewCards.back: The exit has to be practical. A worker should be able to refuse without expert help, social pressure, hidden links, or a process so annoying that delay traps them.

reviewCards.front: Whose welfare is supposed to justify automatic retirement escalation?
reviewCards.back: The chooser's welfare justifies the nudge, not the designer's favorite metric. Higher saving is defensible when it fits what the worker would want under clearer conditions.

reviewCards.front: How would nudge conditions change the way you handle automatic retirement escalation?
reviewCards.back: Nudge conditions say design matters most when choices are hard, rare, delayed, unfamiliar, or poorly mapped. Retirement saving fits that pattern, so payroll design deserves extra care.

reviewCards.front: What are the four Save More Tomorrow design levers named for payroll saving?
reviewCards.back: The four levers are defaults, automatic enrollment, future escalation, and opt-out freedom. Together they make saving easier while keeping refusal inside the design.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice checking whether a helpful path is still easy to refuse. Use Test the Exit before you praise a default, copy a preset option, or ask someone to accept automatic escalation. The move is one question: can the person say no without a fight?

ifThenPlans.context: If a default looks harmless because everyone can technically change it
ifThenPlans.plan: If the default looks harmless, then Test the Exit by walking the refusal path yourself before you defend the design.

ifThenPlans.context: If a choice depends on a future benefit that is hard to picture
ifThenPlans.plan: If the future benefit feels fuzzy, then Test the Exit and rewrite the choice so today's action maps to the later consequence.

ifThenPlans.context: If someone praises a nudge only because the average result improved
ifThenPlans.plan: If the result looks better, then Test the Exit by asking whether refusal stayed cheap, visible, and socially easy.

ifThenPlans.context: If your preferred outcome starts sounding like the chooser's best interest
ifThenPlans.plan: If your own goal gets loud, then Test the Exit by asking what the chooser would want under clearer conditions.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before one real response about money in the next day, run one rehearsal. Stand where you will answer, ask "Could I refuse this without hassle?" and change one word if the answer is no.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of this week, review one choice you made easier for someone else. Name what changed about your skill at testing the exit, and do not keep a daily log.

memorableLines.text: A default is a decision with a head start.
Tomorrow is easier to promise than today.
An opt-out matters only when exit is real.

chapters.title: Naive Investing
chapters.hook: A fund menu slides from printer to inbox, looking helpful until every line asks for a guess.
chapters.counterintuition: What looks like investor freedom is often a hard quiz with a soft deadline. The menu can be open and still steer you toward a crude split, a costly fund, or no choice at all.
chapters.tryThisNow: The next time you feel pulled to split money evenly, set a two-minute timer. Write one sentence comparing one index fund with the menu; name the fee gap.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A good investing menu makes the diversified, low-cost path easy to see and easy to refuse, instead of asking every saver to act like an expert.

breakdown.fastRead: A retirement form can look harmless while it eats a weekend. Claude has a paycheck to protect, a phone near dead, and a fund list that asks him to choose like a portfolio expert before the enrollment window closes. So he does what many people do: he thinks about splitting the money evenly. That feels fair, but it can make the menu, not the investor, choose the risk. Too many doors can make the hallway smaller. The fix is not to scold Claude with more pages. The fix is to shape the menu so the broad, low-cost, diversified route is plain, while the exit remains real.
breakdown.deepRead:
Harry Markowitz gave finance a clean way to think about diversification, and even that does not make an ordinary retirement screen easy. Portfolio theory says the mix of assets matters. In plain words, do not let one bad bet sink the ship. But a defined contribution plan does not hand a tired worker a simple ship; it often hands over a list of funds, fees, and risk labels. Under stress, equal splitting can feel like humility. It is also a clue that the menu is doing too much hidden work.

The mechanism is simple. Hard choices push people toward shortcuts. A long list makes attention thin. Fees sit in small print. Risk arrives later, when the paycheck has long moved on. Delay then picks for you, because the status quo keeps running while you wait. A cheap broad fund can beat an impressive menu. That line is not a stock tip. It is a design point: if the low-cost index fund is the sensible base for many savers, the menu should not bury it among louder choices.

The U.S. SEC's investor material makes this concrete by pointing savers toward diversification and fees, not just fund names. A worker can compare a low-cost index fund with a costly narrow fund because those features connect today's click to later welfare. More disclosure is not automatically better. If Evelyn needs a magnifying glass, a PDF, and a free evening to find the fee, the document has not helped at the decision point. Good choice architecture makes the important comparison visible while the choice is still live.
breakdown.fullRead:
The harder case begins when a helpful shortcut starts acting like a command. A target-date structure can be useful because it bundles diversification into one recognizable path. Pick the rough date when money will be needed, and the fund adjusts the mix over time. That can rescue a saver from a menu that demands expert work. It also creates a new duty for the designer: the person who wants another path must be able to leave without a maze.

This is where Naive Investing stays inside the larger nudge idea. The goal is not to produce the designer's favorite portfolio by any means that works. It is to improve likely welfare by the chooser's own lights. If Wendy wants to hold a different mix because she has other savings, a pension, or a real reason to take more risk, the architecture should let her do that. The nudge earns trust only when refusal is practical.

Harry Markowitz is useful here because he shows the expert contrast. Portfolio theory is not equal parts of whatever happens to be listed. It asks how the pieces fit together. That is why naive equal splitting is such a revealing mistake. It is not a moral failure. It is a normal response to a menu that hides the shape of the choice. When the list is lopsided, an even split can become lopsided too.

Fees sharpen the point. A small annual cost can feel too tiny to matter on the day you enroll, but it keeps taking its bite while the account grows. If the cheaper diversified option is hard to spot, the plan has preserved formal choice while making the useful choice faint. Freedom needs more than a long list. It needs a map that marks the costs a saver is likely to miss.

The U.S. SEC angle helps because it keeps the advice testable. A saver can look for diversification, investment fees, and the role of index funds. Those are not magic words. They are handles for a better comparison. If a plan lists fund names first and costs last, the saver may treat the flashiest fund as the serious one. If the plan puts broad exposure and fees near the front, the same saver can see what the choice is asking.

The overcorrection is just as real. A designer can fall in love with simplicity and push every saver into one neat lane. That is no longer humility about human limits; it is the designer's preference wearing a helpful coat. Guidance curdles when exit becomes theater. The right menu does not erase advanced choices. It makes the plain route legible, keeps fees visible, and leaves the door open for the saver who has a reason to walk another way.

examples.title: Claude's Equal Split
examples.scenario: 1/n sits in Claude's notebook beside the defined contribution plan menu. He has not clicked anything. The scarce thing is attention: read every fund sheet, search for fees, or use the equal split that seems fair enough before his phone dies on the train. The tradeoff fills the whole moment. Each path spends his limited focus in a different way.
examples.whatToDo: Claude writes the equal split as a warning, not a plan. He circles fees, diversification, and the broad base option before he lets the menu spend his attention.
examples.whyItMatters: The scene shows portfolio choice overload in the open. When a rough split brings relief, the menu may be asking a nonexpert to do expert work.

examples.title: Easton's Fee Fork
examples.scenario: The low-fee index fund is plain, and the higher-fee fund has the richer story on the plan comparison page. New hire Easton is torn between two bad options at the enrollment kiosk. Pick the plain fund and worry he missed expert upside, or pick the polished fund and pay more for a promise he cannot test. The U.S. SEC notes on diversification and investment fees make the tension harder, not easier.
examples.whatToDo: Easton compares the fee and diversification columns before the sales story. He marks the cheaper broad fund as the base case, then asks what would justify leaving it.
examples.whyItMatters: A real dilemma keeps the lesson honest. The answer is not fewer words; it is a clearer path from today's fund choice to tomorrow's welfare.

examples.title: Evelyn Hears Markowitz
examples.scenario: "Even the Nobel Prize guy did not make this feel simple," someone says on the phone line, and Evelyn stops highlighting fund names. Wendy, the plan coach, answers without a lecture. "Harry Markowitz gave us portfolio theory, not a blessing for equal slices." Evelyn asks, "So equal is not the same as diversified?" Wendy says, "Only if the pieces already fit."
examples.whatToDo: Evelyn repeats the distinction in her own words. She asks whether the listed funds overlap, then treats equal slices as a question to test.
examples.whyItMatters: The dialogue separates a good instinct from a bad shortcut. Diversification means a working mix, not equal respect for every fund on a screen.

examples.title: Phoebe's Plain Fund
examples.scenario: "Start with the thick packet," the benefits guide says, and Phoebe expects the serious choice to live there. The packet has charts, manager notes, and a confident tone. Then the comparison page loads: the plain index fund shows broad diversification and lower investment fees in one line. The quiet option teaches more than the louder brochure.
examples.whatToDo: Phoebe resets the order of review. She starts with diversification and fees, then reads fund stories only after the basic comparison is clear.
examples.whyItMatters: The reveal breaks the common guess that more documents mean better disclosure. Useful disclosure helps at the moment of choice.

examples.title: Wendy's Exit Thread
examples.scenario:
The clean target-date button sits above the buried fund list, and both are on Wendy's screen.
Wendy: The default is useful.
Nora: Where is the exit?
Wendy: Under "advanced."
Nora: Then it is not an exit yet.
Wendy: Move it beside the default?
Nora: Yes. Help is still help only if no is reachable.
examples.whatToDo: Wendy changes the screen draft so the target-date path and the exit sit together. She treats the opt-out as part of the design, not a footnote.
examples.whyItMatters: The thread keeps the freedom test short. A target-date structure can steer well, but only while refusal stays visible and usable.

examples.title: Nora Restarts Enrollment
examples.scenario: The senior benefits aide at the enrollment help desk loses her voice, and Nora, scheduled only to restock forms, gets the headset with a line already waiting. Her routine is to read fund names aloud. Halfway through, she hears how useless that sounds, stops, and restarts: target-date path, index fund option, fee column, exit link. The pause changes the help.
examples.whatToDo: Nora restarts from the shape of the menu. She names the simple diversified route first, points to fees, and shows how to choose something else.
examples.whyItMatters: The reset is the technique. When overload starts, the useful move is not more fund names; it is a clearer order for comparing them.

questions.prompt: Claude says the retirement menu is fair because every fund remains available. Nora says the setup can still fail. Which reading fits Naive Investing?
choices: Nora is right because a formal menu can overwhelm savers who use crude rules.
Claude is right because options solve the problem once they are listed.
Claude is right because retirement savers should avoid any guided path.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 says portfolio choice overload remains even with formal choice. A long menu can push crude splitting or delay when the architecture is poor.

questions.prompt: Easton thinks a diversified base option is not a nudge unless the plan argues for it. Wendy expects behavior to shift anyway. Who has the stronger read?
choices: Easton is right because only spoken persuasion changes a retirement choice.
Wendy is right because people often follow the easiest route under complexity.
Easton is right because diversification works only after expert coaching.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 supports Wendy. Defaults, salience, and friction can change behavior without a speech, especially when the choice is hard.

questions.prompt: Phoebe leaves the fee comparison for later because she wants a calmer evening to think. What is likely to happen in the meantime?
choices: The current path keeps acting while the hard choice waits.
The delay keeps the investing outcome neutral until she returns.
The extra time removes the need to inspect fees closely.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 treats Phoebe's pause as consequential. A default, status quo, or old allocation can keep acting while fees still matter.

questions.prompt: Evelyn can add either a longer packet or a clearer index-fund comparison to the enrollment page. Which change best follows the mechanism?
choices: She should add a longer packet so every fund has more supporting text.
She should make the index-fund comparison show fees and diversification plainly.
She should remove the comparison so savers make a cleaner private choice.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 favors clearer mapping at the decision point. More documents can fail if the saver cannot use them while choosing.

questions.prompt: Nora likes a target-date path but sees that leaving it requires a hidden form. Which criticism should she make before launch?
choices: The path can stay if the average saver balance rises.
The path can stay if the exit form exists somewhere.
The path should put the no beside the yes before launch.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 says steering needs a practical opt-out. A hidden form is not enough, even when the target-date path may help many savers.

questions.prompt: Wendy wants one independent anchor for why low-cost diversified funds belong in the design discussion. Which source fits that job?
choices: The U.S. SEC material on index funds, diversification, and fees fits that job.
A fictional saver story with realistic fund names fits that job.
A single payroll anecdote about delayed paperwork fits that job.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 names the U.S. SEC as an independent anchor. A real design case carries more weight than an invented or isolated story.

questions.prompt: Claude wants the plan to push the portfolio he personally likes best. Phoebe says that misses the nudge standard. What distinction matters?
choices: The designer's choice matters if the form looks simple to complete.
The designer's choice matters if it raises the average balance.
The chooser's welfare matters, not the designer's favorite outcome.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 asks whether the portfolio path serves the saver rather than Claude's taste. Better design is justified by likely saver welfare, not a designer favorite.

questions.prompt: Easton says a mandate and a nudge are the same once both improve retirement outcomes. Which reply keeps the nudge frame intact?
choices: They match when the expert can prove the suggested fund is better.
They differ when the preferred arrangement remains avoidable.
They match when the plan gives savers a written explanation.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 says the nudge frame depends on an avoidable preferred path. A mandate removes or heavily penalizes alternatives.

questions.prompt: Alice sees a fund list and plans to divide money evenly so no choice feels neglected. What should a choice architect infer first?
choices: The saver has shown a stable preference for equal risk in every fund.
The saver has solved the menu by avoiding any need for design help.
The saver may be using a crude rule because the menu is too hard to use.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 points to overload and crude diversification rules. Equal splitting may reveal an unusable menu, not a well-formed preference.

reviewCards.front: What is portfolio choice overload in plain words?
reviewCards.back: It is what happens when a retirement saver faces a fund menu that is formally open but hard to use. The person may split money evenly, delay, or miss fees because the menu demands expert work.

reviewCards.front: How does Harry Markowitz help you see the flaw in equal fund splitting?
reviewCards.back: Markowitz points toward portfolio theory: the mix matters because the pieces interact. Equal slices of a lopsided menu are not automatically diversified, even if the split feels fair.

reviewCards.front: Why do index funds and fees belong near the front of the investing menu?
reviewCards.back: They give the saver a usable comparison. A broad low-cost fund can make diversification and fees visible before fund stories, brands, or thick packets take over attention.

reviewCards.front: When does a target-date structure stop feeling like a nudge?
reviewCards.back: It stops when leaving it becomes hard, hidden, or costly. The structure can guide a saver, but opt-out freedom has to be practical at the moment of choice.

reviewCards.front: Where does self-control conflict (Ch 2) help here, and where would leaning on it mislead you?
reviewCards.back: It helps explain delay: the calm saver plans, while the tired saver postpones. It misleads if you blame only willpower. Naive Investing also asks whether the menu made the choice too hard.

reviewCards.front: What are the four Naive Investing Design Levers?
reviewCards.back: The four levers are diversification, fees, index funds, and target-date structure. Together they keep the useful path visible without erasing the right to choose another route.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice noticing when a menu is doing hidden work. Check the Menu Shape means you compare the broad low-cost route with the busy list before you split money evenly. The move is not to avoid choice; it is to make the real choice visible.

ifThenPlans.context: If a money menu makes an even split feel like relief
ifThenPlans.plan: If the even split feels soothing, then Check the Menu Shape by asking which fund features the menu made hard to compare.

ifThenPlans.context: If a packet gives you more fund facts but no clearer choice
ifThenPlans.plan: If the packet gets thicker, then Check the Menu Shape by finding the fee and diversification comparison before reading the story.

ifThenPlans.context: If a target-date or default path looks helpful
ifThenPlans.plan: If the path looks helpful, then Check the Menu Shape by finding the exit before you praise the design.

ifThenPlans.context: If your favorite portfolio starts sounding like everyone's best answer
ifThenPlans.plan: If your preference gets loud, then Check the Menu Shape by asking what the chooser would want under clearer fees and easier comparison.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next day, when you feel pulled to choose by equal split, add a ten-minute calendar block. During it, compare fees, diversification, and the exit from the default.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, tally each time you want the even split because a menu is tiring. At week's end, read the number and ask whether the menu, not preference, steered you.

memorableLines.text: Too many doors can make the hallway smaller.
A cheap broad fund can beat an impressive menu.
Guidance curdles when exit becomes theater.

chapters.title: Credit Markets
chapters.hook: You tap a credit offer open, and the fee box waits until your rent money is already spoken for.
chapters.counterintuition: A loan can disclose its APR and still leave you lost. Paper can be honest while the choice stays hard to compare.
chapters.tryThisNow: At your next handoff or transition between tasks, count four cost words in one credit offer. Write one line you would ask aloud about total cost.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Do not ask whether credit terms were merely disclosed. Ask whether APR, fees, timing, and exit are clear enough to compare before you borrow.

breakdown.fastRead:
You are trying to cover a bill, and the card offer looks helpful until the small costs start moving. The APR sits in one place. Fees sit in another. A teaser rate sounds cheap until a late payment changes the story. If rent is due, the easiest route can feel like the only route.

Credit markets hurt people when cost is scattered. The Truth in Lending Act pushed lenders to state an APR, the annual percentage rate, so borrowers could compare credit prices in a common form. That was a real improvement. It was not the whole job. Paperwork is not transparency.

Transparent borrowing means the person choosing can see what the loan is likely to cost in normal use. The design move is simple: put the rate, the likely fee, common language, and side-by-side shopping where the borrower can use them. A cheaper loan should be easy to recognize.
breakdown.deepRead:
The hard part is that credit cost does not arrive as one neat number. A borrower may see an APR, then a late fee, then a billing rule, then a penalty term. Each item is legal information. Together, they can still be a maze. Transparent borrowing asks whether the pieces meet at the moment of choice.

APR disclosure changes the path of least resistance. When every lender uses a common rate, the borrower does not have to translate each offer from scratch. The rate does not solve the whole problem. It is a shared ruler. If Bradley and Maurice compare two offers, the APR gives them one line they can discuss before the sales pitch takes over.

Fee salience is the next lever. A salient fee is a fee you notice while it can still change your plan. A late fee buried in a long agreement is different from a fee placed beside the payment date. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has made credit-card agreements easier to find and inspect, but a searchable pile is still a pile if the borrower cannot see which fee will bite.

Standardized terms do the same work for language. If every lender calls the same charge by a different name, comparison shopping becomes guesswork. Standard words let the borrower ask, "What changes my total cost?" That question does the small work.

The nudge here is not a ban. It is a better map. You can still borrow, walk away, or choose a product with features you value. But the route should not depend on catching a fee after you are already late. Hidden cost is expensive freedom.
breakdown.fullRead:
The Credit CARD Act shows why timing matters. A fee notice can be true and still arrive too late to guide the borrower. If the fee becomes visible only after the habit is set, disclosure has become a receipt for harm, not a warning before it.

That is why credit design keeps returning to the same question: can the borrower compare before committing? APR rules help because they bring a common number into the shopping moment. A searchable federal agreement database helps when credit-card agreements and fees are easier to inspect. The Credit CARD Act points to a later problem: fees, rates, and billing practices need attention because they shape what borrowing costs in real life.

The source idea has four levers: APR disclosure, fee salience, standardized terms, and comparison shopping. Leave one out and the map loses value. APR disclosure gives the shared rate. Fee salience makes costly moments visible. Standardized terms keep lenders from hiding the same charge under different words. Comparison shopping turns the data into a choice among real offers.

Beatrice and Emmett show the difference in plain life. Beatrice checks only the monthly payment and hopes the rest is fine. Emmett asks for the total cost line before he borrows. Neither person is stupid. One setting makes the price easy to feel now and the other delays the pain. Credit design should help the Emmetts of the world without pretending every Beatrice deserves the fee she missed.

Still, the hard edge matters. Transparent borrowing is not permission for a designer to pick any outcome that raises average welfare. A nudge is justified by the chooser's welfare, not the designer's favorite result. If a borrower wants a costly card for a reason she understands, the design should let her keep that choice. Freedom needs a usable exit.

The same boundary protects the policy from becoming a quiet mandate. If refusal is costly, hidden, or slow, the steering is no longer gentle. A credit menu that says "you may leave" but buries the exit behind calls and penalties is not much of an option. The preferred route must remain avoidable in practice.

Transparent borrowing quietly assumes a working market around the borrower. There must be more than one real offer to compare, enough time to inspect terms, and a practical way to refuse. When those preconditions are missing, disclosure alone cannot carry the weight. The form may be cleaner, but the borrower is still trapped.

examples.title: APR Counter Talk
examples.scenario: The envelope glue catches on borrower Bradley's thumb at the credit union counter as he pulls out the credit offer. "This one says low monthly payment," he says. Instructor Maurice points to the Truth in Lending Act box. "Read me the APR." "That is the annual rate, right?" "Yes. Same ruler first, then we talk about fees." Bradley keeps the second offer folded until he finds the APR line.
examples.whatToDo: Bradley reads the APR before the payment pitch. Maurice keeps the talk on a common rate so the offers can be compared before any sales detail takes over.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange shows disclosure doing useful work only when it enters the conversation early. APR is a shared ruler, not a charm against bad borrowing.

examples.title: Fee Search Catch
examples.scenario: The PDF scroll bar skids downward while Kathleen searches a Consumer Financial Protection Bureau credit-card agreement. She is about to close the file because the APR looks fine. Then she notices her own shortcut: she has searched rate, not fees. The missed-rent fear in her stomach changes the next move. She types late fee and reads the billing section before choosing.
examples.whatToDo: Kathleen stops herself before treating one clean number as the whole price. She searches the agreement for fees and billing language while the choice is still open.
examples.whyItMatters: Her recovery shows the core problem. A searchable agreement helps only if the borrower knows which hidden cost to bring into view.

examples.title: Fee Notice Memo
examples.scenario: Joel lowers the stapler before it bites the packet and writes one more memo line. Note: the Credit CARD Act made fees and billing practices harder to hide, but our notice still has to arrive before the borrower acts. Put late fees beside the payment date. Put penalty-rate language beside the teaser rate. Do not let the first clear warning be the bill.
examples.whatToDo: Joel rewrites the memo around timing. He places the fee warning next to the decision point instead of leaving it as a clean paragraph after the fact.
examples.whyItMatters: The memo carries the design move. Disclosure protects choice when it reaches the borrower before the costly habit has already been set.

examples.title: Two Offer Paths
examples.scenario: Flipping the offer pages backward, Beatrice lands on the monthly payment and relaxes. The APR box is above it, but she treats it as legal filler. Across the credit union desk, Emmett starts with the Truth in Lending Act disclosure, copies the APR, then marks the fee line before asking about the payment. Beatrice plans around cash this month. Emmett plans around the price of borrowing.
examples.whatToDo: Beatrice reads the offer from payment to fine print. Emmett reads from APR to fees to payment, so the cheap-looking route has to survive comparison.
examples.whyItMatters: The same disclosure can guide one borrower and miss another. Good design makes Emmett's path easier for Beatrice to follow before money is due.

examples.title: Agreement Reframe
examples.scenario: Pauline has just begun the credit-card agreement when Maurice's call cuts through the speaker. "I hate this," she says. "The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau can help you find the agreement, but it cannot read your week for you," Maurice says. "Do not look for the prettiest number. Look for the number that changes your total cost." Pauline writes fees beside Friday rent.
examples.whatToDo: Pauline repeats Maurice's question and searches the agreement for the fee that could hit her tight week. She ties the document to cash she can picture.
examples.whyItMatters: The reframe makes salience personal. A fee matters when the borrower can see the day it may bite, not only the paragraph where it is named.

examples.title: Classroom Cost Line
examples.scenario: There is not enough class time to read every line, and Maurice knows it, so he circles one blank row on the whiteboard. APR disclosure. Fee salience. Standardized terms. Comparison shopping. A learner asks whether more pages mean better disclosure. Maurice hands out two short offers and says, "Find the cost line you could use before borrowing."
examples.whatToDo: Maurice makes the learners fill one comparison row instead of admire a stack of papers. Confusion becomes the material for practice.
examples.whyItMatters: The lesson separates paperwork from usable disclosure. A borrower needs terms arranged so the next cost can be compared while the choice is alive.

questions.prompt: Bradley has three credit offers, each with long terms and a clean signature line. Which reading best fits transparent borrowing?
choices: The choice is usable once Bradley has several formal options in front of him.
The choice is usable once Bradley receives every document the lender is required to send.
The choice is usable only if Bradley can compare APR, fees, penalties, and timing.
questions.explanation: Transparent borrowing is about usable comparison, not the mere presence of options or paper. Hidden fees and timing can make formal choice hard to use.

questions.prompt: Kathleen compares two card pages before applying. One lender moves the APR line beside the payment estimate; another leaves it in a later packet. Which result is most likely?
choices: Kathleen is more likely to compare the offers because the common rate is now on the easy path.
Kathleen is more likely to ignore the offer because only spoken persuasion changes behavior.
Kathleen is more likely to choose at random because disclosure adds friction by definition.
questions.explanation: APR disclosure can nudge by changing what is easy to notice. The mechanism is salience and friction, not a speech telling Kathleen what to do.

questions.prompt: Joel postpones reading the late-fee line until after he submits the application. What should a careful reader expect?
choices: The delay protects Joel's choice because no fee matters until a bill is due.
The delay keeps Joel neutral because postponed terms do not steer behavior.
The delay may select the current path because the fee stays hidden until change is harder.
questions.explanation: Postponement is not neutral. When a hard detail is delayed, the status quo often keeps moving and the fee becomes visible too late.

questions.prompt: Beatrice receives more pages about a card, but each fee has a different name across offers. Which response uses standardized terms well?
choices: She should align the same charges under common words so today's choice maps to later cost.
She should trust the longer packet because more documents usually mean better disclosure.
She should focus on the opening payment because future cost is too uncertain to compare.
questions.explanation: Standardized terms help when consequences are hard to compare. More pages do not help if Beatrice cannot match today's words to later costs.

questions.prompt: Emmett likes a comparison table, but leaving the recommended card requires a long call and a fee. Who has the better read?
choices: Beatrice says the table protects freedom because the average borrower will do better.
Emmett says the table protects freedom only if refusing it remains practical.
Pauline says the table protects freedom because all steering is softer than a ban.
questions.explanation: Comparison shopping stays liberty-preserving only when exit is realistic. A welfare gain alone does not settle the freedom question.

questions.prompt: Maurice is planning an adult class on transparent borrowing and needs a real case for the first worksheet. Which source anchor fits that job?
choices: The Truth in Lending Act and APR show a real disclosure rule for consumer credit.
A made-up lender can show the same rule as long as the invented offer is detailed.
A general story about confusing loans can replace a real institution if the moral is clear.
questions.explanation: The Truth in Lending Act and APR supply a real anchor. Transparent borrowing needs actual credit-market design, not only a plausible invented story.

questions.prompt: Pauline already understands APR from one example. Why bring in the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and credit-card agreements?
choices: One example is enough once it proves that disclosure can be written in legal form.
A second example matters mainly because it gives readers another institution to memorize.
The CFPB anchor shows the same design problem in agreements and fees, not one isolated story.
questions.explanation: The CFPB case gives an independent anchor for the same mechanism. It keeps the lesson from resting on one anecdote about APR alone.

questions.prompt: A designer wants to steer borrowers to the card the company prefers because it raises repayment rates. Which objection fits transparent borrowing?
choices: The design is fine if the company's preferred card creates a cleaner average outcome.
The design must be judged by the borrower's welfare, not the designer's favorite result.
The design should avoid all steering because any menu order counts as coercion.
questions.explanation: A nudge is defended by welfare as the chooser would judge it. Designer preference is not enough, and steering is not automatically coercion.

questions.prompt: A credit site highlights one safer card and hides every other card behind extra penalties. How should that design be classified?
choices: It is a nudge because the highlighted card probably improves borrower outcomes.
It drifts toward a mandate because alternatives are costly enough to be hard to refuse.
It remains neutral because every card still appears somewhere on the site.
questions.explanation: The larger nudge structure requires the preferred arrangement to remain avoidable. Heavy penalties make refusal too costly to count as a practical opt-out.

reviewCards.front: What is transparent borrowing in plain words?
reviewCards.back: Transparent borrowing means a borrower can see the likely cost before choosing. APR, fees, penalties, and timing have to be arranged for comparison, not scattered across a packet.

reviewCards.front: Why is paperwork not the same as transparency?
reviewCards.back: Paperwork can disclose facts without making them usable. Transparency asks whether the borrower can compare the cost at the decision point, while the choice is still open.

reviewCards.front: What are the four Credit Markets design levers?
reviewCards.back: The four levers are APR disclosure, fee salience, standardized terms, and comparison shopping. Together they turn scattered credit terms into a map a borrower can use.

reviewCards.front: How does the Truth in Lending Act / APR example ground transparent borrowing?
reviewCards.back: It gives a real credit-market case where standardized APR disclosure tries to make offers comparable. The lesson is not that APR solves everything, but that shared measures matter.

reviewCards.front: Why does practical opt-out matter in credit design?
reviewCards.back: A design can steer without becoming a mandate only if refusal stays realistic. If leaving the preferred route is costly, hidden, or slow, the choice is no longer meaningfully open.

reviewCards.front: In one sentence, how would you connect portfolio choice overload (Ch 7) to transparent borrowing's core move?
reviewCards.back: Both ideas say a formal menu is not enough: investing needs legible diversified choices, and credit needs a total cost line that lets borrowers compare before committing.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice turning scattered credit terms into one sentence you can compare. Write the Total Cost Line by naming the APR, the fee most likely to hit, and when that fee would arrive. The skill is not doing finance like an expert. It is refusing to let the easiest number stand for the whole price.

ifThenPlans.context: If an offer leads with a low payment
ifThenPlans.plan: If the payment is the first number you notice, then write the Total Cost Line before reading the pitch again.

ifThenPlans.context: If a fee appears after several pages
ifThenPlans.plan: If the fee is buried, then move it into the Total Cost Line and ask when it could hit your account.

ifThenPlans.context: If two offers use different words for charges
ifThenPlans.plan: If the terms do not match, then rewrite both charges in the same plain words before comparing them.

ifThenPlans.context: If leaving the recommended option feels hard
ifThenPlans.plan: If refusal takes a call, penalty, or delay, then add that cost to the Total Cost Line before calling the design a nudge.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, at one credit or subscription choice, write one line: "The cost I can compare is ___, and the fee that could surprise me is ___."
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, swap your first credit-check habit. Instead of scanning for the lowest payment, write the Total Cost Line first. Compare the first half and second half of the week.

A cheaper loan should be easy to recognize.
