chapters.title: Privatizing Social Security: Smorgasbord Style
chapters.hook: A bright fund list looks like freedom; 1 of 4 levers, the default, often does the deciding.
chapters.counterintuition: Despite the appeal of a giant investment menu, freedom can shrink when the list is too hard to use. A clean default and easy exit can protect choice better than more pages.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before you start your next money form, say aloud: "If the menu runs long, I will ask for the default, the fee, and the exit before choosing."
chapters.keyTakeaway: When a retirement menu gets crowded, protect choice with a limited menu, a default fund, low-cost diversification, and an opt-out people can use.

breakdown.fastRead: Claire hears a man in the Sweden pension office mutter that the ad has already chosen for him. She has been fixing the letter by adding more fund detail. Halfway through the sentence, she sees her own error. The problem is not only missing facts. It is a fund menu that asks busy savers to act like full-time investors. More choice can hide the choice that matters. A good retirement menu gives people real room to choose, then protects them from being steered by noise, delay, and brand shine.
breakdown.deepRead:
The mechanism is simple: when a choice is hard, the easiest path starts acting like an adviser. In Sweden's premium pension system, broad fund choice looked respectful. It also meant that a saver could face a fund menu with weak mapping. A name, a fee, and a glossy pitch did not clearly show what the choice would mean for retirement. That is why the four levers matter: limited menu, default fund, low-cost diversification, and opt-out. They do not end choice. They make the first path less likely to punish a normal person for being busy.

Oscar sees the same logic inside his own head. The instruction says, "Choose the best fund," and his mind first treats that as a test of intelligence. Then the wrong turns start. Pick the fund with the boldest ad. Split money across names that sound different. Wait until the choice feels clear. Each move feels reasonable for a moment. Each one lets the menu, the ad, or delay do quiet work. A default is the answer delay will sign.

The 401(k) case gives the second anchor. Automatic enrollment changes what delay selects. If the box starts blank, waiting often means no retirement saving. If enrollment starts as the preset path and refusal is plain, waiting often means saving. The choice still belongs to the worker, but the path of least resistance has changed. That is the whole smorgasbord idea: offer a spread, but do not pretend every spread is equally kind to the person holding the plate.
breakdown.fullRead:
Blake is handed the benefits role because the usual plan manager is out sick. The 401(k) screen is waiting, and every setting carries a cost. Leave the box blank, and people who mean to save can slide into doing nothing. Preselect automatic enrollment, and some employees may feel the firm has leaned on them. This is the live tension under retirement menu design. The form cannot avoid influence. It can only choose which influence it will own.

Sweden's Premium Pension Authority shows why this question travels beyond one country. Privatized accounts do not become wise just because they offer many funds. A public system that sends citizens into fund choice has already built a choice environment. It has decided how many funds appear, which option sits first, what the default does, how fees are shown, and how hard exit feels. If those parts are sloppy, the system can preserve formal choice while leaving real choice to advertisements and inertia.

Nash tests the opt-out link and finds the liberty question hiding in the small print. A better average outcome is not enough by itself. The chooser's welfare has to be the reason for the design, and refusal has to remain practical. Exit is freedom only when ordinary people can find it. If opting out takes insider knowledge, a long phone call, or a form hidden three screens down, the nudge has changed character. It may still move behavior, but it no longer has the same claim to respect choice.

Emilia's first page holds the four levers in plain view. A limited menu cuts the noise before the saver is lost. A default fund answers the question that delay would answer anyway. Low-cost diversification means spreading risk without asking each person to become an expert. Opt-out keeps the door open for the person who has a good reason to take another path. None of these levers requires the planner to know every saver perfectly. They require the planner to admit that menus have power.

Annabelle's frozen pension page is where the common myth breaks. The myth says more options equal more freedom. That sounds clean until her screen freezes under the weight of another fund description and the only thing she remembers is the ad she saw last week. At that moment, the long list has not made her more sovereign. It has made the visible cue more powerful.

A lawmaker asking whether to privatize Social Security is in a different fight. Menu design cannot prove that a country should create individual retirement accounts in the first place. If that is the real question, a neat default fund does not settle it. The claim here starts after that gate: if citizens are asked to choose inside private accounts, the menu should not turn confusion into costly inertia. Build the smorgasbord so people can eat well, decline plainly, and still reach the door.

examples.title: Claire Hears the Ad
examples.scenario: "The ad already chose for him," a clerk says at the next desk in the Sweden pension office, and policy writer Claire stops above the Swedish Premium Pension Authority letter. During final copy review, she has been adding another paragraph about fund choice in the retirement system. The overheard line shows her own error: more text may just make the loudest fund name win.
examples.whatToDo: Claire crosses out the extra paragraph. She rewrites the letter around the default fund, the fee cue, and the clear opt-out before she adds any more fund detail.
examples.whyItMatters: Her correction protects choice by changing the moment of use. A saver needs a usable path, not a thicker official letter beside the same hard menu.

examples.title: Oscar's Silent Menu
examples.scenario: "Pick the fund that fits you," the screen says, and Oscar feels accused by the Sweden premium pension portal. Best return? Lowest fee? Familiar name? He almost splits the retirement accounts across funds that sound different. Then he notices the trick in his own thinking: the fund menu has made variety feel like wisdom, though he has not compared the choices well.
examples.whatToDo: Oscar stops treating the long list as proof of skill. He looks for the default fund and the low-cost diversified option before touching the advertised names.
examples.whyItMatters: The scene shows how naive allocation can feel careful. A menu can make a weak rule look like personal judgment when mapping is poor.

examples.title: Emilia Budgets Attention
examples.scenario: The short guide sits beside the giant fund catalog on policy planner Emilia's Premium Pension Authority desk. Before the mailing goes out, she has one page of attention to spend on Sweden's retirement fund choice. The tradeoff is not action yet. It is where the reader's eye should go first: the limited menu, the default fund, the fee, or the full sprawl.
examples.whatToDo: Emilia assigns the first page to the default fund, low-cost diversification, and exit. The full list stays available, but it no longer gets the first claim on attention.
examples.whyItMatters: Planning the menu is already a nudge. The first page can help a saver map today's click to later welfare, or it can bury that cue.

examples.title: Blake Gets the Screen
examples.scenario: The benefits manager is home sick, and Blake gets the 401(k) setup screen with no clean option. He must choose where the default goes. If he leaves automatic enrollment blank, delay may choose no retirement saving for busy workers. If he preselects default funds, some will say the firm pushed too hard. The cursor blinks.
examples.whatToDo: Blake preselects automatic enrollment and puts the opt-out beside it in plain language. He accepts steering only with a visible, realistic refusal path.
examples.whyItMatters: The dilemma keeps the liberty question honest. A default can help with delay, but only if workers can leave without a search mission.

examples.title: Aline and Nash Test Exit
examples.scenario: Enrollment analyst Aline is clicking the default funds box during a 401(k) enrollment review call while Nash is still reading the opt-out copy. "Leave it under disclosures," Aline says. "Workers can find it." Nash answers, "Then delay is not the only thing we changed." Aline pauses. "Move the exit next to automatic enrollment?" Nash says, "Yes. If it is freedom, make it findable."
examples.whatToDo: Aline moves the opt-out link beside the 401(k) automatic enrollment choice. Nash checks the wording as if a new worker were reading it in a hurry.
examples.whyItMatters: Their exchange separates nudging from trapping. The default may favor retirement saving, but the worker's no must stay practical.

examples.title: Annabelle's Jammed Packet
examples.scenario: The printer tray sticks halfway at the Premium Pension Authority print station, and packet clerk Annabelle expects the fix to be more pages for Sweden's premium pension fund menu. During final packet review, the next call proves her guess wrong. The caller is not asking for every retirement account detail. He asks what happens if he does nothing, what the default costs, and how to leave it.
examples.whatToDo: Annabelle cuts the packet back to the usable questions first. The full fund list remains, but the default, cost cue, and exit move to the front.
examples.whyItMatters: The reveal breaks the more-information myth. Disclosure helps only when a saver can use it at the moment the choice bites.

questions.prompt: Claire says Sweden's premium pension problem is solved once citizens receive a large fund menu. Emilia says the menu itself still needs design. Who has the better read?
choices: Claire is right because formal options make the policy problem disappear.
Claire is right because any official fund list counts as enough guidance.
Emilia is right because poorly structured options can overload savers.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 says retirement menu design remains a problem when options are hard to use. A formal list alone can still overwhelm or mislead.

questions.prompt: Aline shortens a 401(k) menu and makes the preset path clearer. Oscar says that is not a nudge unless she argues workers into it. Which view fits the source logic?
choices: Oscar is right because only direct persuasion changes retirement behavior.
Oscar is right because workers ignore paths unless every fund is explained.
Aline is right because the easiest route can shape behavior under complexity.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 says defaults, salience, and friction can influence behavior without argument. The path of least resistance matters.

questions.prompt: Blake closes a retirement menu after seeing too many fund names. He tells himself the pause is neutral because he has not clicked anything. Which outcome should worry him first?
choices: Waiting will improve the choice because extra time may sharpen judgment.
Waiting will let a default or status quo answer while he postpones.
Waiting will pause every setting until Blake makes an active pick.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 makes Blake's non-click a live outcome. Delay can leave an implicit result in force, even when the chooser feels undecided.

questions.prompt: Annabelle wants pension savers to connect today's choice with later welfare. Which change best follows the design mechanism?
choices: She foregrounds a low-cost diversified path that is easier to compare.
She adds every disclosure page so the full record is available.
She removes cost cues so savers rely on their own fund research.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 favors clearer mapping through low-cost diversification. More documents do not help if the saver cannot use them at the choice point.

questions.prompt: Nash likes a default fund but finds that opting out requires a buried form and a long call. Which criticism is strongest?
choices: The design is fine if the default improves the average saver result.
The design is fine if the full opt-out rule appears somewhere online.
The design loses its liberty claim when refusal is not realistic.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 says opt-out protects freedom only when exit is practical. Better averages or hidden disclosure cannot carry the whole defense.

questions.prompt: Oscar wants to ground a retirement-menu lesson in a real case rather than a made-up saver. Which anchor belongs in the lesson?
choices: He should use Sweden's premium pension case with its public fund choice.
He should use any imagined worker who faces too many finance terms.
He should use a generic shopping story with many products on a shelf.
questions.explanation: Fact 6 names Sweden as a real-world anchor with observable design features. A hypothetical or shopping scene weakens the factual grounding.

questions.prompt: Claire says the Sweden case alone carries the whole lesson. Blake points to 401(k) automatic enrollment. Why does his point matter?
choices: It gives an independent case where the same menu-design pressure appears.
It proves all retirement accounts should use the same fund provider.
It replaces the Sweden case with a separate workplace-only lesson.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 says 401(k) automatic enrollment supplies a second anchor for the same design problem. It does not erase Sweden or prove all plans identical.

questions.prompt: Emilia wants the default fund chosen for the outcome she finds easiest to defend. Annabelle says the standard is narrower. Which standard fits?
choices: The designer may choose the outcome that makes the agency look prudent.
The menu should serve the saver, not the designer's favorite metric.
The designer may pick any result if exit exists in the paperwork.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 separates the chooser's welfare from designer preference. The point is not the agency's favorite metric or a paper-only exit.

questions.prompt: Aline says a mandate and a nudge are the same if both raise retirement saving. Nash disagrees. What distinction should he make?
choices: A mandate improves outcomes only when savers like the rule afterward.
A nudge keeps the preferred path avoidable without heavy penalty.
A nudge removes weak options so savers cannot make costly errors.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 marks retirement nudges by the exit they preserve. The preset path may steer, but it must stay avoidable; mandates close or punish other routes.

reviewCards.front: Why can a large retirement fund menu reduce usable freedom?
reviewCards.back: A large menu can make the saver rely on ads, familiar names, or delay. Usable freedom needs the choice to be clear enough for an ordinary person to compare and refuse.

reviewCards.front: What are the four design levers in smorgasbord-style retirement accounts?
reviewCards.back: The levers are limited menu, default fund, low-cost diversification, and opt-out. Together they reduce overload while keeping a path for people who want another choice.

reviewCards.front: Why is postponing a pension choice not neutral?
reviewCards.back: Postponement usually leaves something in force. A default, blank box, status quo, or ad memory can answer while the saver feels as if no choice has been made.

reviewCards.front: What does Choice Architecture (Ch 5) get WRONG if you applied it naively to Sweden's pension menu?
reviewCards.back: A naive use would say any arranged menu counts as enough design. The stricter test asks whether the menu helps the chooser's own welfare and keeps opt-out practical.

reviewCards.front: When does a default fund stop being a nudge and start looking like a shove?
reviewCards.back: It crosses the line when refusal is hard to find or costly to use. The default can steer, but the exit must be plain enough for a busy saver.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice spotting the moment a menu starts doing the choosing for you. Ask the Menu Question: what is the default, what does it cost, and how do I leave? The skill is not picking the perfect fund. It is refusing to let confusion, ads, or delay pick first.

ifThenPlans.context: If a money form offers a long list of options
ifThenPlans.plan: If the list starts to blur, then Ask the Menu Question before reading further: name the default, the cost cue, and the exit.

ifThenPlans.context: If a default is already selected for you
ifThenPlans.plan: If a box is preselected, then Ask the Menu Question and check whether leaving the path is as visible as staying on it.

ifThenPlans.context: If you feel tempted to delay a retirement choice
ifThenPlans.plan: If delay feels neutral, then Ask the Menu Question and state what answer delay will sign if you do nothing.

ifThenPlans.context: If you are designing a form for someone else
ifThenPlans.plan: If another person must use your menu, then Ask the Menu Question from their side and move the exit where they can find it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: The next time a financial menu appears today, say aloud: "I replace reading every option first with finding the default, the cost, and the exit."
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, explain Ask the Menu Question to one person in your own words. Use Sweden's premium pension menu or a 401(k) default as the example.

chapters.title: Prescription Drugs: Part D for Daunting
chapters.hook: Can you pick a drug plan while your refill waits and every premium looks alike?
chapters.counterintuition: It seems kind to offer every Medicare Part D plan and let people sort the rest. In fact, choice needs a translator when the wrong match can raise drug costs.
chapters.tryThisNow: During your next conversation about a hard menu, slide the actual form between you, count four quiet breaths, then write one sentence naming the first comparison to show.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When a choice is hard, keep the options real but make the match plain: show the costs that fit the person's own drugs, pharmacy, and exit path.

breakdown.fastRead: Jenna keeps one palm on the pharmacy counter while the clerk searches for her refill. Her phone is at one percent, the charger is gone, and the plan list on the screen looks like a wall of premiums. Medicare Part D began in 2006 to help pay for prescription drugs, yet the help arrived as a menu of private plans. Jenna does not need a lecture on freedom. She needs the list to start with her drugs, her pharmacy, and the costs she will actually face. A big menu can hide a bad fit. The nudge is the translation: keep choice, but make the likely match easier to see.
breakdown.deepRead:
Henry slides a wrinkled drug list across the pharmacy counter and taps the line where his refill price changed. The Medicare Plan Finder asks for that list because a premium alone cannot answer his real question. A plan can look cheap at the top and still miss the drugs he uses, the pharmacy he visits, or the costs that appear after the first easy number.

The mechanism is simple. Hard choices make people grab the visible piece. In Part D, the visible piece may be the monthly premium. The less visible pieces are the formulary, which is the list of covered drugs, the deductible, the pharmacy terms, and the donut hole, the coverage gap named in the source case. If those pieces stay scattered, delay chooses for the person. If the screen maps drugs and pharmacy to expected drug costs, the same freedom becomes usable.

CMS, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, points to the better design through Medicare.gov and Plan Finder. It does not erase the menu. It asks for the facts that make the menu personal. That is why disclosure alone is weak here. More pages can still leave Henry guessing. A short path from drug list to plan cost gives the choice a shape his body can use while he is tired at the counter.

The design levers are plan matching, drug list disclosure, annual review, and intelligent assignment. Each one answers a different failure. Match the plan to the person. Ask for the drugs before the plan is chosen. Check again when the drugs change. Use a default only when the person can leave it. Good help starts with the chooser's life.
breakdown.fullRead:
Blair has already circled the lowest premium when she notices the pharmacy name is wrong. The mark looks small, but it changes the whole choice. Her plan was to save money. Her shortcut almost sent her toward a plan that did not fit the place where she gets her prescriptions.

Blair's pencil mark sets the boundary. A nudge is not just any clever push that improves an average. The claim is narrower. A better design should improve welfare by the chooser's own lights. In plain words, it should help Blair get what she would want if the plan were easier to understand. It should not smuggle in the designer's favorite answer.

Blair's opt-out line matters as much as the match. Intelligent assignment can help when a person is lost in the plan menu. It can be fair to assign a likely fit based on drugs, pharmacy, and drug costs. But the assignment stays in nudge territory only if refusal remains practical. If Blair needs a long call, expert words, or a pile of forms to leave the suggested plan, the design has become something heavier than help.

A refill changes, and last year's good plan can stop fitting. Drug use changes. Pharmacies change. Premiums change. A review can protect a person who would otherwise drift with last year's plan. It can also annoy people who already chose well. The test is not whether the review creates one neat answer for everyone. The test is whether it catches real mismatches without making people feel trapped.

You can read every word on a Part D page and still not know what to do. A plan can disclose premiums, covered drugs, deductibles, formularies, and the coverage gap, yet still ask too much at once. You may know each word and still not know which plan fits. That is the difference between information and mapping. Information says what exists. Mapping shows how this choice will land on your refill, your pharmacy, and your bill.

Ask who carries the cost before you praise the map. If the menu is all freedom and no map, the person carries it. If the map becomes a locked route, freedom has been traded away. A nudge earns trust only while refusal stays close. That sentence is easy to say and hard to build into a health system.

Here is what it costs. Ella sits beside Hunter at a diner booth after helping him enter his drug list. She wants to say, "This is the best plan." Instead, she turns the paper so he can see the premium, the pharmacy, the expected drug costs, and the exit line. The slower answer takes more space. It gives up the clean pride of one expert pick. Better help costs the pride of total choice. Hunter leaves with a plan, but also with the burden of knowing what would make him change it.

examples.title: Jenna Restarts the List
examples.scenario: Jenna's thumb pauses above the pharmacy keypad during a plan-review visit at the pickup counter. As a Medicare Part D enrollee, she sees the shape of 2006: private prescription drug plans, a donut hole, and too many ways to be wrong. She sets the card flat, asks for her current drug list, and starts again from the refill she came to pick up.
examples.whatToDo: Jenna stops the routine that starts with plan names. She restarts with the drugs, the pharmacy, and the costs that would touch her next refill.
examples.whyItMatters: The pause protects choice from becoming a guess. A Part D plan is only useful when the person can see how it fits the medicine in hand.

examples.title: Henry's Paper Bag
examples.scenario: Sliding the paper bag across the counter, Henry hears the pills rattle before he reads the receipt. The Medicare Plan Finder screen beside the register asks for a drug list, a pharmacy, and a premium. The paper curls under his wrist. No speech is needed; the small bag shows why a plan name alone is too thin.
examples.whatToDo: Henry keeps the receipt beside the Plan Finder fields and checks the drug list before staring at the premium again.
examples.whyItMatters: The vignette makes the map concrete. A premium is not the whole price when the drug list and pharmacy decide what the person pays.

examples.title: Yvonne and Ella at Medicare.gov
examples.scenario: Yvonne is naming the cheapest premium when Ella's printer coughs and stops. "Read the CMS line again," Ella says. "Medicare.gov wants drug costs after my pharmacy, not before." Yvonne looks back at Plan Finder. "So we enter the drugs first?" "Yes. Then the price belongs to my list, not to a brochure."
examples.whatToDo: Yvonne follows Ella back to the order on Medicare.gov. She enters the drugs and pharmacy before treating any cost as meaningful.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange keeps help humble. CMS Plan Finder works best when the helper lets the person's own drugs organize the comparison.

examples.title: Blair Uncircles Premium
examples.scenario: The lowest premium is already circled on Blair's annual review worksheet at the enrollment desk. As a Part D enrollee, she notices the formulary page is still folded shut. The 2006 design problem is back in pencil: premium first, donut hole later, real coverage last. She rubs the circle until the paper thins.
examples.whatToDo: Blair catches her own shortcut before it hardens. She uncovers the formulary, checks the drug fit, and then lets the premium reenter the comparison.
examples.whyItMatters: The recovery matters because the error is ordinary. People often grab the visible number before checking the parts that make the plan work.

examples.title: Bailey's Review Memo
examples.scenario: The office memo has one blank line where the next step should be. Bailey writes: "CMS Plan Finder should begin with Medicare.gov drug costs, not last year's plan name. Ask for current drugs and pharmacy. Show the expected cost. Mark the exit path in the same paragraph, so assignment stays easy to refuse."
examples.whatToDo: Bailey turns the memo into a usable order of work. Current drugs, current pharmacy, expected costs, and exit all appear before anyone praises the match.
examples.whyItMatters: The memo keeps annual review from becoming paperwork theater. It asks whether the match still fits and whether refusal is still practical.

examples.title: Hunter Hears the Shortcut
examples.scenario: "Just pick the cheapest premium," someone says from the next booth, and Hunter stops sorting the refill receipts. Ella writes premium at the top of one napkin and drug list, pharmacy, and Plan Finder on another. Hunter follows the first napkin and gets a quick answer. He follows the second and sees why the answer changes.
examples.whatToDo: Hunter tests both paths instead of arguing. Ella keeps the Plan Finder path tied to the drug list and pharmacy, while the premium-only path stays visibly thin.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast shows why more choice is not the same as better help. The useful path maps the menu to the person's actual prescription life.

questions.prompt: A Part D menu lists many private plans and assumes choice alone solves the problem. Which result should a careful reader expect?
choices: People will sort the plans well because the menu proves the options are available.
People will need fewer aids because adding plans reduces the work of matching.
People may still mismatch because the menu can be too complex to use well.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 says the problem is Medicare choice overload. Formal options can still be unusable when complexity makes good matching hard.

questions.prompt: Henry says the easiest Part D route will shape choices even without a speech. Bailey says only direct advice can count as a nudge. Who has the better read?
choices: Henry is right because defaults and friction can steer behavior under complexity.
Bailey is right because a nudge must persuade people with an explicit argument.
Bailey is right because health choices respond only to expert recommendations.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 says plan matching changes the path of least resistance. A nudge can work through defaults, salience, and friction.

questions.prompt: Yvonne keeps putting off entering her drug list because she has not chosen a plan yet. What is the hidden risk in that delay?
choices: The delay keeps every option equally open until she feels ready to compare.
The delay proves the drug list matters less than the premium printed first.
The delay may leave a default or old plan doing the choosing for her.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 warns Yvonne that no click is still a path. An old plan or implicit default can keep operating while she waits.

questions.prompt: Blair's annual review packet lists new plan terms, but she still cannot see what her refills will cost later. Why is a clearer cost map the better fix?
choices: Annual review helps when it connects today's plan to later drug costs.
Annual review helps when it gives people more pages than last year.
Annual review helps when it waits until people ask for expert help.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 says review improves choice by mapping options to later welfare. More documents alone can fail at the decision point.

questions.prompt: At a help desk, Jenna sees an assigned Part D plan that fits many drug lists but takes a long call to leave. How should she judge it?
choices: It remains a clean nudge because the average match may improve.
It risks coercion because refusal is no longer practical.
It becomes neutral because assignment replaces active choice.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 says intelligent assignment protects freedom only when exit is realistic. A costly refusal changes the design's character.

questions.prompt: A writer wants to explain choice overload with an invented plan menu. Another writer uses Medicare Part D in 2006. Which anchor is stronger?
choices: The invented menu is stronger because it avoids messy policy details.
Medicare Part D is stronger because it gives real plans and design features.
The invented menu is stronger because the lesson works without institutions.
questions.explanation: Fact 6 says Part D grounds the claim with named institutions and observable design features. A bare hypothetical is weaker evidence.

questions.prompt: After naming the Part D plan menu, Yvonne opens Medicare Plan Finder and enters a drug list. What does that second anchor add?
choices: It shows the same design problem through a separate comparison tool.
It replaces the Part D case because one policy example is enough.
It proves the drug list matters only for people using Medicare.gov.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 says Plan Finder supplies an independent anchor. The same mechanism appears outside one isolated case.

questions.prompt: Bailey likes a plan because it lowers the office's workload. Ella asks whether it helps the chooser by the chooser's own lights. Who is closer to the source?
choices: Bailey is closer because lower workload is enough to justify a design.
Ella is closer because the nudge must serve the chooser's welfare.
Bailey is closer because designer preference settles hard comparisons.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 puts Ella's question first: does the match help the enrollee? Office convenience cannot stand in for chooser welfare.

questions.prompt: Hunter sees a default Part D match and a required plan rule that both improve average outcomes. How should Part D design answer?
choices: They are the same because both move people toward a better average result.
They are the same because expert control is part of choosing drug coverage.
They differ because the preferred arrangement must remain avoidable.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 says the preferred arrangement remains avoidable in the nudge framework. A mandate makes alternatives much costlier.

reviewCards.front: Why can a large Medicare Part D menu still fail the person choosing?
reviewCards.back: A menu can offer real options while hiding the match. If the person cannot connect plans to drugs, pharmacy, and likely drug costs, choice becomes guesswork.

reviewCards.front: How does plan matching nudge without giving a speech?
reviewCards.back: It changes the path of least resistance. When the screen starts with the person's drugs and pharmacy, the easier route is also the route that compares real costs.

reviewCards.front: Why is delaying the drug list not a neutral move?
reviewCards.back: Delay leaves something else in charge, often an old plan or default. The drug list has to enter early because it turns a generic menu into a personal comparison.

reviewCards.front: When does intelligent assignment stop feeling like a nudge?
reviewCards.back: It crosses the line when exit is hard. A suggested Part D match can preserve freedom only if the person can refuse it without expert help or a long fight.

reviewCards.front: What makes annual review better than another stack of plan documents?
reviewCards.back: Annual review earns its keep when it maps today's drugs and pharmacy to later costs. More paper alone does not help if the person cannot use it at the choice point.

reviewCards.front: Recall self-control conflict (Ch 2): where does Blair's premium shortcut show planner versus doer?
reviewCards.back: Blair's circled premium shows it. Her quick doer wants the easy visible number, while her planner needs the slower check against formulary, pharmacy, and future drug costs.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice making hard choices start with the facts that make them personal. Use Map the Match First when a menu looks fair but feels foggy. The move is to put the person's own list, place, and exit path before the shiny headline number.

ifThenPlans.context: If a menu feels fair because it has many options
ifThenPlans.plan: If the menu is large, then Map the Match First by naming which personal facts must sort the options before anyone chooses.

ifThenPlans.context: If someone wants to postpone the hard comparison
ifThenPlans.plan: If delay sounds harmless, then Map the Match First by asking what default or old path will take over while everyone waits.

ifThenPlans.context: If a default looks helpful on average
ifThenPlans.plan: If the default looks smart, then Map the Match First by tracing the exit path before you praise the assignment.

ifThenPlans.context: If your preferred outcome starts sounding like the person's best interest
ifThenPlans.plan: If your goal gets loud, then Map the Match First by asking what the chooser would want after seeing the costs clearly.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before one real menu choice in the next day, move the page beside the item at stake. Write one sentence naming the personal facts that should sort first.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Use Map the Match First three times this week at widening gaps. First map a small menu, later a money choice, and last a choice where another person must keep an easy no.

Good help starts with the chooser's life.
Better help costs the pride of total choice.

chapters.title: How to Increase Organ Donations
chapters.hook: A donor prompt slides through a license renewal, and silence begins to count as an answer.
chapters.counterintuition: Why does a life-saving wish fail at a plain form? Because you can favor donation and still let the default cast the vote.
chapters.tryThisNow: During your first coffee, count the first five preset choices you meet in apps or forms; mark which answer stands if you stop there.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Donation defaults can save more lives when the form asks clearly, sets a wise starting path, and keeps refusal easy to find.

breakdown.fastRead:
A license form moves across a counter, and the donor line waits near the signature. One person checks it. Another means to, then leaves it blank. A third never sees the line at all because the clerk is rushing. Silence still signs forms.

You may care about organ donation and still lose the choice to the setup. A default is the answer that takes effect when nobody acts. In donation, that answer can be opt-in, opt-out, or a direct required choice. The moral wish is only part of the story. The path on the form decides how easy that wish is to record.
breakdown.deepRead:
The gear is small: hard choices drift toward the path with the least friction. Organ donation is hard to think about. It asks you to picture death, family grief, and a future patient you will never meet. So the license counter or registry page does quiet work before you speak. If donation needs an extra box, delay often means no. If refusal needs an extra step, delay often means yes. A good default leaves the exit door in daylight.

Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein made this point vivid in their work on donation defaults. Their question was not whether people are generous. It was whether a form can hide generosity by making the generous act the harder route. This is why the design levers must stay distinct: opt-in, opt-out, mandated choice, and family consent. Opt-in asks you to join the registry. Opt-out starts from donation and lets you refuse. Mandated choice asks for an answer now. Family consent asks how the choice works when loved ones are in the room.

Allison sees the same lesson in a license office. Earlier, the donor line sat below a stack of routine renewals, and blank space carried the day. Later, the form asks each applicant to pick yes or no before the renewal can close. That change does not force donation. It stops delay from pretending to be a view. The reader's test is plain: find the answer that wins when attention fails, then ask whether that answer serves the chooser by the chooser's own lights.
breakdown.fullRead:
Spain matters because it keeps the story from becoming box worship. Its donation system is often linked with presumed consent, but the stronger lesson is mixed: consent rules work inside a system that also uses transplant coordination and family process. A law can set a starting point. It cannot, by itself, replace trust at a bedside.

That is the hard edge of donation defaults. Higher donation rates are not the only value. A nudge is defensible when it helps people do what they would endorse after a real chance to choose. It is not defensible when it hides refusal, surprises families, or treats the designer's target as the chooser's welfare. If Marc cannot find the opt-out line, the form is no longer just helping his better wish survive delay. It is making refusal cost more than it should.

Mandated choice has a special appeal here. It respects the fact that some people strongly support donation, some strongly refuse, and many postpone the whole thought. A direct question at license renewal can be blunt, but blunt can be kind when the alternative is silent drift. The form can ask, record the answer, and let the person move on. It turns a buried preference into a marked one.

Family consent keeps the policy human. A registry entry may be clear to the state and still feel shocking to a loved one. For that reason, the prompt should be salient before a crisis. Salient means hard to miss. A clear prompt, plain words, and a visible refusal path make later family talks less like ambush and more like carrying out a known choice. Donation design fails when families feel ambushed.

The same lesson reaches ordinary forms. If you have missed one message in a flooded group chat, you know how a small piece of design can decide what gets seen. A donor choice buried under routine license steps can suffer the same fate. The answer may matter more than anything else on the page, yet the page can make it feel like another checkbox.

There is also a trust cost after the form leaves the counter. A family member who never heard the donor wish may read the registry as paperwork from strangers. A coordinator then has to do two jobs at once: honor the recorded choice and keep the family from feeling pushed aside. Better design starts that work earlier, while the chooser is alive and the question can still be plain.

Do not use a default when people lack a fair chance to see it, understand it, and leave it. In that case, do the opposite: ask directly, slow the form down, and make no answer count as no answer. Defaults are powerful because attention is scarce. That power earns trust only when refusal stays practical.

examples.title: Finn's Two Forms
examples.scenario: Finn has a checked donor box in one hand and a blank donor line in the other, and both are sample driver's license forms. At the training desk, the instructor asks which organ donor registry answer will be recorded if the applicant hurries. Finn says the blank line proves refusal, then catches himself: an opt-in form may record delay, not belief.
examples.whatToDo: Finn rewrites his training note. He separates a true no from an unanswered opt-in box, then asks clerks to point out the donor line before the license signature.
examples.whyItMatters: The classroom mistake carries the whole design problem. A blank answer can look like choice while the form is really letting friction choose.

examples.title: Allison Closes the Renewal
examples.scenario: The senior clerk is covering testing, and Allison gets the driver's license renewal counter with the organ donor registry queue already backing up. Earlier opt-in forms let the donor box sit blank while the license printed. The later screen will not close until Allison asks yes or no. Same counter, same rush, one changed rule: delay no longer writes the answer.
examples.whatToDo: Allison asks the donor question out loud and records the answer before printing the license. She treats no as valid, but she no longer treats silence as no.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast shows what mandated choice adds. It preserves refusal while stopping a rushed license visit from quietly burying support for donation.

examples.title: Donovan's Spain Audit
examples.scenario: Policy analyst Donovan keys Spain into the audit column in a health ministry archive room while the next row is still blank. He is reviewing organ donation files after reading Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein on default rules. The first note says presumed consent. The file that changes his mind says transplant coordination and family process sit beside it. The box alone did not explain the system.
examples.whatToDo: Donovan revises the audit finding. He keeps presumed consent in the report, but pairs it with coordination and family consent before drawing a policy lesson.
examples.whyItMatters: The quiet find blocks a lazy default story. Spain shows that the starting rule matters most when the institution around it earns trust.

examples.title: Marc at the Kiosk
examples.scenario: Driver Marc tugs his license card from the motor vehicle kiosk during his license renewal in the license office lobby, and the slot grips it halfway before flashing the organ donor registry screen. He thinks yes, donation is right. Then he thinks, wait, why is refusal behind another tap? If opt-out is fair, it should not hide. Maybe the default helps people like him follow through. Maybe it also needs a plain door out.
examples.whatToDo: Marc checks whether the no is as visible as the yes before accepting the default. He lets the helpful path stand only after the exit is clear.
examples.whyItMatters: His thoughts protect the liberty claim. Opt-out can steer toward donation, but the steering changes character when refusal becomes hard to use.

examples.title: Elaine's Four Levers
examples.scenario: Four levers. Elaine writes them at the top of the reply-all draft before any policy meeting begins: opt-in, opt-out, mandated choice, family consent. The inbox wants a quick answer about presumed consent. Her scarce attention has to go elsewhere first, across the whole donor registry design, because one lever cannot carry the moral work alone.
examples.whatToDo: Elaine plans the agenda around all four levers. She gives each a question, then refuses to let presumed consent swallow the whole donor policy debate.
examples.whyItMatters: The planning scene keeps the menu complete. Donation defaults work through a system, not through one magic setting on a registry form.

examples.title: Jacqueline's Bedside Call
examples.scenario: Transplant coordinator Jacqueline draws the consent packet toward her in the hospital hallway, then stops before the signature line. In Spain's organ donation system, presumed consent and transplant coordination meet the family at the bedside. One path presses the legal default and risks making grief feel overruled. The other waits for comfort that may not come in time. She must decide how to ask without treating trust as delay.
examples.whatToDo: Jacqueline slows the first sentence and names the recorded default, then asks what the family understood before she moves the packet closer.
examples.whyItMatters: The dilemma shows why family consent belongs in the framework. A default can help only if the people living the moment do not feel ambushed.

questions.prompt: A license office says its donor registry is fair because every driver can mark yes or no. Thierry thinks the form itself still matters. Who reads the problem better?
choices: The office reads it better because listed options settle the donor choice for drivers at renewal.
The office reads it better because registry forms should avoid steering drivers at the counter.
Thierry reads it better because the form can make one answer harder.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 says formal options are not enough when the architecture makes a choice hard to use. The bare-options view misses how the registry path works.

questions.prompt: When an online donor page starts with donation selected, Marc says only a speech from a clerk could change behavior. What is the stronger read?
choices: The selected answer can matter because it changes the easiest route.
The clerk's speech is required because forms cannot steer a donor choice online.
The selected answer matters only after drivers study every registry rule first.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 says friction and defaults can steer without direct persuasion. Marc's speech-only view ignores the force of the easiest route.

questions.prompt: Allison watches a driver leave the donor question for later, sure no real answer has been given. Which result should worry her?
choices: Waiting keeps the donor decision open until the driver studies the issue later.
Waiting lets the default or old registry status make the practical choice.
Waiting improves the donor decision because the driver avoids a rushed counter answer.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 says delay is not neutral. While the driver waits, some default or status quo still governs the record.

questions.prompt: Finn proposes a thicker donor packet at license renewal. Donovan proposes one clear yes-or-no prompt tied to the registry result. Which design fits the mechanism?
choices: Finn's packet fits because more pages give drivers more donor disclosure at renewal.
Finn's packet fits because hard choices need more background before any prompt.
Donovan's prompt fits because it maps today's answer to the registry result.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 favors usable mapping over more paper. The prompt connects today's answer to the later registry outcome at the moment of choice.

questions.prompt: A transplant team likes presumed consent but hides the refusal process in a separate office visit. Which objection best protects opt-out freedom?
choices: The design is sound if donation numbers rise after the presumed-consent change.
The design is sound if staff can explain the refusal process later.
The design loses its defense when refusal becomes costly enough to block exit.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 says freedom depends on a realistic opt-out. Better outcomes do not justify a refusal path that ordinary people cannot use.

questions.prompt: Elaine wants to teach donation defaults with a made-up registry story. Marc says Eric Johnson gives the lesson firmer ground. Why is Marc right?
choices: A real anchor gives named actors and design features to inspect.
A real anchor proves every country should copy the same donor rule.
A real anchor removes the need to test how the registry works.
questions.explanation: Fact 6 makes Eric Johnson a grounding anchor, not a shortcut to one universal rule. The value is that the design features can be checked.

questions.prompt: Thierry claims the donor-default lesson rests on one study. Allison points to driver's license renewal and the organ donor registry. What does that add?
choices: It makes the story more vivid while leaving the mechanism tied to one case.
It shows the design problem in another setting with real forms.
It proves registry staff should focus on licenses rather than family consent.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 says the license registry is an independent anchor. It reduces overfit to one case without replacing the other levers.

questions.prompt: A policy memo praises whichever donor rule gives officials the highest number. Jacqueline asks whose welfare the design serves. Which standard is right?
choices: Jacqueline is right because the nudge must serve choosers' own welfare.
The memo is right because designers may pick the result they prefer.
The memo is right because donation counts settle the welfare question.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 asks whose interests the donor rule serves. A higher count matters, but it cannot replace the driver's or family's welfare standard.

questions.prompt: Donovan says a hard mandate and a donor default are the same once both raise donations. Finn disagrees. Which difference matters?
choices: The mandate matters less because it can be written in plainer language.
The default stays avoidable, while a mandate heavily restricts other paths.
The default matters less because it works only when no family is involved.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 draws the organ-donor boundary around practical exit. Donation may be favored, but a nudge differs from a mandate while leaving remains easy.

reviewCards.front: What are the four design levers for increasing organ donation?
reviewCards.back: The four levers are opt-in, opt-out, mandated choice, and family consent. Each changes a different part of how a donor answer is asked, recorded, or honored.

reviewCards.front: Why can a blank donor box fail to mean real refusal?
reviewCards.back: A blank box can record delay, hurry, or confusion. In an opt-in system, the form may count silence as no even when the person supports donation.

reviewCards.front: How does Spain complicate a simple presumed-consent story?
reviewCards.back: Spain points beyond the legal default. Presumed consent works with transplant coordination and family process, so trust and execution are part of the result.

reviewCards.front: Which matters more for organ donor registration, transparent borrowing (Ch 8) or donation defaults, and why?
reviewCards.back: Donation defaults matter more here because the choice is often made by what happens when attention fails. Transparent borrowing helps compare costs, but the donor case turns on the recorded default and usable refusal.

reviewCards.front: When does an organ-donation nudge stop being liberty-preserving?
reviewCards.back: It stops when refusal is hard to find, costly to use, or surprising to the family. A helpful starting path needs a visible and practical exit.

reviewCards.front: Why is mandated choice different from opt-out?
reviewCards.back: Mandated choice asks for a yes or no and records that answer. Opt-out starts from donation unless refusal is registered, so delay has a different effect.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a form offers a preselected answer, then Test the Recorded Default by naming what happens if you stop and where the exit sits.

ifThenPlans.context: If a group praises a policy only by its higher count
ifThenPlans.plan: If a group praises a policy only by its higher count, then Test the Recorded Default by asking whose welfare the count is meant to serve.

ifThenPlans.context: If a hard choice is easy to postpone
ifThenPlans.plan: If a hard choice is easy to postpone, then Test the Recorded Default by marking the answer that delay will select.

ifThenPlans.context: If someone calls a default harmless
ifThenPlans.plan: If someone calls a default harmless, then Test the Recorded Default by walking through the refusal path as if a tired person had to use it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For one day, count the first five defaults you meet in ordinary forms or apps. Beside each, write the answer that wins if you do nothing.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Keep a daily three-column log for a week: form or app, recorded default, exit path. At week's end, circle the default you trusted least and why.

A good default leaves the exit door in daylight.

chapters.title: Saving the Planet
chapters.hook: 1 home energy report lands, and you see your private electricity use beside your neighbors'.
chapters.counterintuition: Saving the planet is not only a sermon about caring more, but a design job. Make the harm visible while a real choice stays open.
chapters.tryThisNow: Within the next 24 hours, the first time your calendar opens, write "carbon" in the margin beside your next bill-review slot.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Environmental nudges work when they make hidden harm visible, compare choices fairly, and leave refusal practical instead of pretending small cues can solve climate alone.

breakdown.fastRead:
Why does a lower thermostat feel private until a home energy report compares it with neighbors? The answer is feedback. Climate harm is distant, spread out, and hard to see from one switch or bill. A household can use more electricity and never feel the carbon dioxide in the room. Hidden costs need visible handles.

That is why Hunt Allcott's work on home energy reports matters. The report does not shout. It shows electricity use beside a neighbor norm, so a vague concern becomes a concrete comparison. A private bill can teach a public habit.

The practical puzzle is how to save attention when the planet's costs arrive late. The useful design levers are feedback, social comparison, salience, and pricing limits. They help only when the person can still say no.
breakdown.deepRead:
Carbon dioxide does not tap you on the shoulder when the dryer runs twice. That silence is the mechanism. When a cost is far away, spread across many people, and measured in terms you do not use at home, attention slides past it. You keep the light on, the old setting stays, and the effect hides inside a later total.

Feedback gives the choice a reply. Social comparison tells you how your use looks beside a group you can picture. Salience means the important part is easy to notice at the choice point. Pricing limits remind the designer that steering becomes suspect when refusal is too costly. Those four levers matter because plain concern is weak in the face of a busy day.

Opower made this visible with home energy reports that compared electricity use with neighbors. Kira does not need a speech about virtue when the report already shows her home above the local line. She can see the gap before she turns the heat up again. The comparison works within limits. It puts a blurry public cost next to a private habit.

The U.S. EPA greenhouse gas equivalencies tool solves a second problem. Tons of carbon dioxide can feel like a math word with no handle. An equivalency turns the amount into a familiar comparison. That does not make every choice easy, but it lets you map a technical unit onto life you can picture.

Small feedback can open a large choice. It cannot replace power grids, prices, rules, or clean technology. A nudge earns its place when it makes a live choice clearer, not when it pretends climate policy is only a better letter.
breakdown.fullRead:
Adele sees the danger when the utility team wants to celebrate a tiny drop in electricity use as if the planet has been handled. The reports helped. The neighbor line got attention. Yet the coal plant, the old apartment wiring, and the cost of new equipment did not vanish because a household saw a smiley face.

This is the harder angle. Environmental feedback is useful because the harm is hard to feel. It is also easy to oversell because the same invisibility lets a designer claim too much. If the only tool is a report, the burden slides onto households that may have the least room to change.

The home energy report works best when the next action is within reach. Turn down a setting. Notice a heavy-use appliance. Compare this month with a neighbor norm. The report loses force when the person rents a drafty unit, cannot replace the heater, or pays a bill shaped by a building they do not control. Feedback needs a reachable next move.

The EPA equivalency idea has the same strength and weakness. It can make carbon dioxide less ghostly. A number becomes a comparison the reader can picture. But a comparison is not a policy. If carbon looks familiar and the practical path stays blocked, the design has produced awareness without power.

That is why the opt-out condition matters here too. A green default on an energy plan can help if it matches what many customers would choose under better attention. It becomes a shove when the exit is buried, costly, or vague. Freedom shrinks when refusal is only theoretical.

Pricing limits add another hard edge. A price can make hidden environmental costs show up while the hand is still on the choice. But a price that a wealthy household treats as a cue may hit a low-income household as a wall. The same signal can teach one person and trap another.

So the claim stays narrow. Use feedback when the harm is hidden. Use social comparison when people need a peer norm. Use salience when a technical cost needs a plain face. Use pricing limits with care, and check that the person still has a workable exit.

The move misleads the public official who wants a cheap substitute for serious climate policy. For that role, a nudge can become cover for avoiding infrastructure, rules, and technology. It can also hide who has no practical room to respond. Saving the planet needs visible choices, but it also needs choices people can actually afford to make.

examples.title: Nicole's Neighbor Line
examples.scenario: Nicole is trimming the home energy report text when the complaint queue pings. She expects anger at the neighbor comparison. Hunt Allcott's work says social norms can move electricity use, but the line still feels risky. The first reply surprises her: the customer wants to know why her house is above nearby homes, not why the utility mentioned neighbors.
examples.whatToDo: Nicole keeps the neighbor line and makes the next action plain. She links the comparison to one appliance check instead of adding another lecture about climate.
examples.whyItMatters: The reveal shows why feedback works. A hidden electricity habit becomes usable when a household can see its own use against a norm.

examples.title: Adele's Carbon Text
examples.scenario:
The comment window is closing on the city energy notice, and neighborhood volunteer Adele works from a parked car in the driveway with her phone screen bright.
Adele: "Tons sounds like a truck scale."
Jacques: "Use the U.S. EPA equivalency."
Adele: "So the number gets a familiar comparison?"
Jacques: "Yes. Give the unit a handle before people vote."
examples.whatToDo: Adele swaps the bare carbon dioxide figure for a greenhouse gas equivalency and keeps the source name with the comparison.
examples.whyItMatters: The thread shows salience in miniature. A technical measure can guide choice only when the person can picture what the measure means.

examples.title: Kira Restarts Opower
examples.scenario: The Opower mockup on the design studio wall makes every apartment look average during the report review. Opower reviewer Kira holds a red marker; her routine is to add another tip box, but the page is already crowded. She stops, clears the extra copy, and restarts with the neighbor comparison at the top. Electricity use gets one clear contrast before advice begins.
examples.whatToDo: Kira removes the spare tips and makes the neighbor comparison the first thing a household sees on the home energy report.
examples.whyItMatters: The cleared page makes feedback usable. It loses power when it competes with clutter, so the report must protect the comparison.

examples.title: Jacques Hears Tons
examples.scenario: "Nobody knows what a metric ton feels like," someone says behind Jacques at the public comment desk, and the clerk's pen slows. The notice says carbon dioxide, energy, and projected savings. The paper is neat. The room is quiet. Beside the form, the U.S. EPA equivalency turns the same carbon amount into a comparison people can picture.
examples.whatToDo: Jacques leaves the technical term in place, then writes the equivalency beside it so the number has a plain companion.
examples.whyItMatters: The vignette keeps the detail small. Salience is not more noise; it is the right comparison sitting where confusion would start.

examples.title: Heather And Cameron
examples.scenario: "Show them the neighbor line first," Heather says during the utility program phone call, and manager Cameron stops scrolling through boilerplate. "That feels nosy." "Hunt Allcott's home energy reports worked because electricity use had a social norm." "So the report is not a scold?" "No. It shows the gap and the next step."
examples.whatToDo: Cameron moves the social comparison above the general savings copy and adds one clear action below the electricity-use gap.
examples.whyItMatters: The dialogue separates feedback from shame. A report can make a cost visible without turning the household into a bad-person story.

examples.title: Sandrine's Exit Fix
examples.scenario: The opt-out slider drifts toward locked while Sandrine previews the green energy plan screen. She catches her own wording: "standard plan available after checkout." That is not a real exit. She moves the standard plan beside the green default, shows the price difference, and deletes the extra step.
examples.whatToDo: Sandrine changes the screen so refusal is visible before checkout. She keeps the green default, but puts the price and standard option in the same view.
examples.whyItMatters: Her recovery protects the nudge's freedom claim. A green default is different from a mandate only when leaving it is practical.

questions.prompt: Nicole says the utility has done enough because every customer can pick an energy plan. Cameron expects the same page to keep failing. Which reading fits environmental feedback?
choices: Nicole is right because option lists solve the environmental choice once plans are available.
Nicole is right because choice stays clear when the utility avoids neighbor comparisons.
Cameron is right because hidden environmental costs still need clear feedback and comparison.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 says formal options are not enough. Environmental harms are distant and invisible, so the setup needs feedback and social comparison.

questions.prompt: Adele thinks a home energy report can steer behavior without arguing for a moral duty. What is the best reason?
choices: People often follow the easiest clear route when a choice is complex.
People change only after a report states the environmental case directly.
People ignore defaults and friction once they know every option exists.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 supports Adele. Feedback, salience, defaults, and friction can shape the easy route without a persuasive essay.

questions.prompt: Kira postpones the neighbor-comparison line because the report already has many tips. What is likely to happen while the line waits?
choices: The old energy habit keeps running because delay leaves the status quo in place.
The household choice stays neutral because no new comparison has been shown.
The tips become stronger because postponement gives readers more time.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 makes Kira's postponed comparison consequential. Waiting can leave a default or status quo active while the hard comparison stays unseen.

questions.prompt: Jacques can add either a longer carbon appendix or a U.S. EPA equivalency beside the energy choice. Which change best matches salience?
choices: He should add the appendix so careful readers can inspect every technical detail.
He should remove carbon language so residents can focus on the monthly charge.
He should place the equivalency beside the choice so the consequence is easier to compare.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 favors clearer mapping at the decision point. More documents can fail when readers cannot use them during the choice.

questions.prompt: Sandrine likes the green default but sees that leaving it requires a buried checkout step. Which criticism should she make?
choices: The default is acceptable because it may improve average environmental welfare.
The default needs a practical exit before the steering remains defensible.
The default is neutral because the standard plan still exists somewhere.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 says welfare gains do not settle the question. Steering becomes coercive when refusal is costly or hard to find.

questions.prompt: Heather wants a real anchor for a claim about environmental feedback. Why use Hunt Allcott's home energy reports instead of a made-up household?
choices: They supply named research, observable report design, and electricity-use behavior.
They avoid the need to explain feedback, social norms, or energy choices.
They prove any neighbor comparison works in every environmental setting.
questions.explanation: Fact 6 says Hunt Allcott grounds the claim with real actors and observable design features. A hypothetical can sound plausible without testing the mechanism.

questions.prompt: Adele already has the Opower example and wants to stop there. Jacques points to the U.S. EPA equivalency case. Who has the better read?
choices: Adele does because one clear anecdote is enough when it fits the lesson.
Jacques does because the EPA case shows carbon mapping outside one neighbor-report program.
Adele does because extra cases make the environmental mechanism less concrete.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 supports Jacques. The U.S. EPA example keeps the lesson from leaning only on Opower and shows the carbon-mapping problem in a separate tool.

questions.prompt: Cameron wants the report to maximize the utility's preferred green outcome. Nicole asks whose welfare justifies the nudge. What should guide the design?
choices: The design should follow the utility's goal when the climate benefit is easy to measure.
The design should follow the designer's preference when customers miss hidden costs.
The design should help choosers by their own lights, not just serve the designer's target.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 ties nudges to chooser welfare. A design can make hidden costs visible, but designer convenience is not the justification.

questions.prompt: Sandrine compares a green plan default with a rule that removes the standard plan. Both raise enrollment, so which distinction matters for nudges?
choices: They match when enrollment rises and the climate outcome improves.
The default keeps the standard plan reachable; the rule takes that path away.
They match when customers get clear notice before the plan changes.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 asks whether the green default still has a usable off-ramp. Keeping the standard plan reachable makes it a nudge; removing or punishing it turns into mandate territory.

reviewCards.front: What problem does environmental feedback solve for a household choice?
reviewCards.back: It gives a visible reply to a cost the household cannot feel directly. Electricity use, carbon dioxide, and later climate harm need a bill, comparison, or map before they can guide action.

reviewCards.front: How does a U.S. EPA greenhouse gas equivalency help a reader choose?
reviewCards.back: It turns an abstract carbon amount into a familiar comparison. The reader still chooses, but the consequence is easier to picture at the moment it matters.

reviewCards.front: Why do Hunt Allcott's home energy reports use neighbor comparison?
reviewCards.back: The neighbor line gives electricity use a social norm. A household can see whether its use is high or low instead of treating the bill as a private number with no benchmark.

reviewCards.front: When does an environmental nudge start to look coercive?
reviewCards.back: It starts to look coercive when refusal is costly, hidden, or vague. A green default can steer, but the standard option must be visible and practical to choose.

reviewCards.front: How would you restate choice architecture (Ch 5) in your own words, then use it on environmental feedback?
reviewCards.back: Choice architecture is the setup around a choice. Here, that setup should make carbon and electricity feedback visible, compare options fairly, and keep opting out easy.

reviewCards.front: How do feedback, social comparison, salience, and pricing limits work together?
reviewCards.back: One gives the choice a reply, one adds a peer norm, one makes the cost easy to notice, and one checks price plus exit. The set makes hidden harm usable without turning guidance into force.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice making the environmental cost visible before you choose. Use the Make Hidden Carbon Visible move: find the hidden cost, place one comparison beside it, and check that refusal or a lower-impact path is still practical.

ifThenPlans.context: If a bill shows only dollars and no use pattern
ifThenPlans.plan: If a bill hides the pattern, then Make Hidden Carbon Visible by adding one comparison beside the total before you pay it.

ifThenPlans.context: If a carbon dioxide number feels too abstract to picture
ifThenPlans.plan: If carbon dioxide floats past you, then Make Hidden Carbon Visible with a U.S. EPA greenhouse gas equivalency before you decide.

ifThenPlans.context: If a green default is already selected
ifThenPlans.plan: If the green path is preselected, then Make Hidden Carbon Visible by checking the price, the standard option, and the exit before accepting it.

ifThenPlans.context: If a home energy report comparison leaves you feeling scolded
ifThenPlans.plan: If the social norms line feels like blame, then Make Hidden Carbon Visible by asking which electricity use action is reachable.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, the first time an energy choice comes up, use Make Hidden Carbon Visible on that bill or plan screen. Check the usage pattern, price, standard option, and exit before choosing.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, rehearse the move on one real bill, plan screen, or appliance choice. Add one comparison, make the hidden cost visible, and check the exit.
